Pharma Industry.content:
Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries Company
(
TADAWUL:4016
) stock is about to trade ex-dividend in four days. Typically, the ex-dividend date is two business days before the record date, which is the date on which a company determines the shareholders eligible to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade can take two business days or more to settle. Thus, you can purchase Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries' shares before the 2nd of September in order to receive the dividend, which the company will pay on the 15th of September.
The company's next dividend payment will be ر.س0.80 per share. Last year, in total, the company distributed ر.س1.38 to shareholders. Last year's total dividend payments show that Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries has a trailing yield of 2.1% on the current share price of ر.س64.75. If you buy this business for its dividend, you should have an idea of whether Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries's dividend is reliable and sustainable. So we need to investigate whether Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries can afford its dividend, and if the dividend could grow.
Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.
Dividends are usually paid out of company profits, so if a company pays out more than it earned then its dividend is usually at greater risk of being cut. Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries is paying out just 24% of its profit after tax, which is comfortably low and leaves plenty of breathing room in the case of adverse events. That said, even highly profitable companies sometimes might not generate enough cash to pay the dividend, which is why we should always check if the dividend is covered by cash flow. It paid out an unsustainably high 229% of its free cash flow as dividends over the past 12 months, which is worrying. It's pretty hard to pay out more than you earn, so we wonder how Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries intends to continue funding this dividend, or if it could be forced to cut the payment.
Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries paid out less in dividends than it reported in profits, but unfortunately it didn't generate enough cash to cover the dividend. Were this to happen repeatedly, this would be a risk to Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries's ability to maintain its dividend.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?
Companies with consistently growing earnings per share generally make the best dividend stocks, as they usually find it easier to grow dividends per share. If earnings fall far enough, the company could be forced to cut its dividend. With that in mind, we're encouraged by the steady growth at Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries, with earnings per share up 8.3% on average over the last five years. Earnings have been growing at a steady rate, but we're concerned dividend payments consumed most of the company's cash flow over the past year.
Many investors will assess a company's dividend performance by evaluating how much the dividend payments have changed over time. In the past two years, Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries has increased its dividend at approximately 27% a year on average. It's encouraging to see the company lifting dividends while earnings are growing, suggesting at least some corporate interest in rewarding shareholders.
To Sum It Up
Has Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries got what it takes to maintain its dividend payments? Middle East Pharmaceutical Industries delivered reasonable earnings per share growth in recent times, and paid out less than half its profits and 229% of its cash flow over the last year, which is a mediocre outcome. Overall, it's not a bad combination, but we feel that there are likely more attractive dividend prospects out there.

Worth looking at what previous legal action actually did to Meta rather than reaching for tobacco. The FTC's record five billion dollar privacy fine in 2019 was met with the stock rising, because it came in below fears and removed an open question. GDPR was designed to constrain large platforms and increased their share of the European ad market, because compliance cost fell hardest on small intermediaries. The FTC's antitrust case, the one that could genuinely have broken the company up, was decided in Meta's favour last November. The only thing that ever meaningfully hurt the business was Apple changing a tracking default, and Meta out-spent that too, while the ad-tech firms that could not afford to rebuild disappeared. The pattern is not that Meta survives regulation. It is that regulation keeps costing its smaller competitors more.

Earlier in 2026, Chugai Pharmaceutical began rolling out an agentic AI platform across its drug discovery workflow and entered a collaboration with Phylo to apply this technology to single-cell data, human genetics, and disease biology.
This move uses Chugai’s strong profitability to fund AI-driven R&D aimed at earlier, more precise target selection that could reshape how its future pipeline is built.
We’ll now examine how Chugai’s agentic AI deployment with Phylo could influence its investment narrative around R&D productivity and diversification.

Chugai Pharmaceutical Investment Narrative Recap
To own Chugai, you need to believe its strong profitability and Roche partnership can be converted into a broader, more resilient pipeline before key products mature. The Phylo agentic AI roll out directly targets the short term concern around R&D productivity and diversification, but its impact on near term revenue dependence on Hemlibra and Actemra is still uncertain and may not materially change the immediate patent and pricing risks.
The Phylo collaboration, which embeds the Biomni Lab AI platform into Chugai’s discovery workflow, sits alongside recent filings to expand Tecentriq and Enspryng indications. Together, these moves connect an AI enabled research engine to tangible late stage assets, giving investors a clearer link between today’s cash generation, tomorrow’s potential indications, and the effort to offset exposure to pricing pressure and upcoming patent expiries.
Yet, against this promising AI story, investors should be aware of how exposed Chugai still is to concentrated revenue and ongoing drug price pressure...

Pharma Industry.content:
Drugmakers may bear sole responsibility for overpricing essential medicines under NPPA proposal
iStock
Synopsis
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority aims to hold drug manufacturers solely accountable for the excessive pricing of essential medications. This initiative could shield retail chemists and hospitals from legal repercussions concerning pricing infractions. Manufacturers are likely to challenge the proposal, alleging it is uncompromising and unjust. Previously, substantial penalties have been levied against drugmakers for such transgressions.
By
Vikas Dandekar
,
ET Bureau
Aug 29, 2026, 06:00:00 AM IST
Follow us
Mumbai: The
National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority
(NPPA) has proposed drugmakers be held solely responsible for overpricing of essential medicines, potentially exempting retail chemists and hospitals from prosecution risks. Manufacturers are likely to contest this move.
ADVERTISEMENT
For medicines that are part of the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), an upward or downward price revision is implemented from the day the revision orders are issued.
Also Read:
Demand for vaccines surges as H1N1, other influenza cases see a sharp rise
However, pharma industry sources told ET retailers often continue selling medicines at prices higher than what's prescribed in the revised orders.
According to the current provisions of Para 26 of
DPCO 2013
, "no person is permitted to sell any formulation to any consumer at a price exceeding the price specified on the current price list or price indicated on the label of the container or the pack thereof, whichever is less."
A meeting of senior government officials earlier this week noted the revision to the draft guidelines was proposed in 2016 as an amendment to the
Drug Price Control Order
(DPCO) 2013.
ADVERTISEMENT
Sources told ET that officials proposed to delete the specific provision which says: "Wherever there is strong evidence to establish that the dealer or retailer selling overpriced medicines has done so with the knowledge of the price reduction, NPPA will also take action against such dealer along with the manufacturers."
The deletion applies to billings made by nursing homes and hospitals as well, besides chemists.
ADVERTISEMENT
ADVERTISEMENT
Also Read:
Biocon arm gets Japan nod for cancer drug pegfilgrastim biosimilar
Unfair and Unjust: Industry
ADVERTISEMENT
Top sources in the pharmaceutical industry said drugmakers are likely to oppose this unilateral move. Industry sources said the watchdog's proposal is biased and unfairly punishes drugmakers for violations by other parties.
"Even if retailers or hospitals are found wilfully selling medicines at prices before the revisions are made, they will not be prosecuted. This is not justified and needs to be thought through," a senior industry official told ET.
ADVERTISEMENT
Under various provisions, the government is empowered to recover the overcharged amount along with a 15% penal interest.
Until March 2026, the pricing watchdog levied cumulative penalties of ₹8,447 crore, of which ₹1,582 crore has been recovered from drugmakers, its data shows. The body has thus far filed 2,737 cases of pricing violations.
The government follows a market-based pricing formula to fix the prices of essential medicines.
However, a recent parliamentary committee report has urged the government to switch to a cost-based pricing formula since the system lacked transparency and had limitations.
"The committee is of the view that pricing based on average retailer margins fails to deliver fair, sustainable pricing for novel interventions," the panel said in its recommendations. "The committee believes that pricing governance must strike a balance between the cost-based model and a value-based model to ensure both affordability and industry sustainability."

Preferred Price to Book of 4.7x: Is it justified?
Ascletis Pharma trades at a P/B ratio of 4.7x, which looks demanding when set against its small revenue base and ongoing losses, even after the recent share price rebound.
The P/B ratio compares the HK$10.10 share price to the book value per share on the balance sheet. For early stage biopharma companies like Ascletis Pharma, investors often focus on this metric because earnings are negative and revenue is still limited. As a result, book value and the asset base can become a key yardstick.
For Ascletis Pharma, that 4.7x P/B is described as expensive relative to the Hong Kong biotechs industry average of 3.7x. At the same time, it is flagged as good value against a much higher peer average of 80.1x, which suggests the peer group includes companies trading at very large multiples. The mixed signal is that the stock carries a premium to its immediate industry but sits at a heavy discount to a wider peer set that appears priced far more aggressively.

Worth looking at what previous legal action actually did to Meta rather than reaching for tobacco. The FTC's record five billion dollar privacy fine in 2019 was met with the stock rising, because it came in below fears and removed an open question. GDPR was designed to constrain large platforms and increased their share of the European ad market, because compliance cost fell hardest on small intermediaries. The FTC's antitrust case, the one that could genuinely have broken the company up, was decided in Meta's favour last November. The only thing that ever meaningfully hurt the business was Apple changing a tracking default, and Meta out-spent that too, while the ad-tech firms that could not afford to rebuild disappeared. The pattern is not that Meta survives regulation. It is that regulation keeps costing its smaller competitors more.

Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical stock has had a difficult long term run, with the share price down about 74.4% over the past 5 years, yet current valuation checks still suggest investors are not getting a clear bargain. Recent gains have come alongside important product news, which makes the current pricing worth a closer look rather than a simple reaction to headlines.
The roughly 74.4% decline over 5 years points to a company that has already seen a major reset in investor expectations. This can leave remaining shareholders focused on execution risk and capital needs.
The recent accelerated FDA approval for Genglycos as Ultragenyx’s first gene therapy can support long term growth expectations. The risk is that the company may still face uncertainty around uptake, pricing and the cost of building out its rare disease portfolio.
The broader valuation checks give a mixed picture rather than a clear bargain or clear overvaluation for Ultragenyx, with a
value score of 4
that sits in the middle of the range.
The issue now is whether Ultragenyx’s current share price fairly reflects the balance between its newly approved therapy, its long track record of share price declines, and the still mixed valuation signals.

Has Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical Run Too Far on Sales?
P/S is often a useful way to compare Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical with other biotechs because many companies in the sector still report losses and do not have a meaningful P/E ratio.
Ultragenyx trades on a P/S of about 3.6x, which is below the wider biotech industry average of 12.9x and also below the peer group average of 6.6x. On the surface that suggests the market is applying a discount to each dollar of Ultragenyx revenue compared with many other biotechs.
The fair P/S ratio for Ultragenyx is estimated at 2.6x based on its size, risk profile and financial characteristics. That is lower than the current 3.6x level, which suggests the stock may be overvalued on this framework even though it trades at a discount to the broader industry. Despite the recent approval of Genglycos and any impact that may have on sentiment, the current P/S still reflects a higher valuation than the fair ratio estimate.
On this preferred P/S multiple framework, Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical stock currently appears overvalued relative to its estimated fair ratio benchmark.

Marquis Who's Who Honors Randolph Greasham for Expertise in the Pharmaceutical Sector
Press Release
August 28, 2026
Randolph Greasham is recognized for decades of success in scientific research at Merck & Co.
Share This Story:
Over the course of his career at Merck & Co., Dr. Greasham has received several awards and honors that reflect his impact on industrial microbiology and biotechnology.
MOUNTAINSIDE, NJ, August 28, 2026 /24-7PressRelease/
-- Randolph Greasham has been selected for inclusion in Marquis Who's Who. As in all Marquis Who's Who biographical volumes, individuals profiled are selected on the basis of current reference value. Factors such as position, noteworthy accomplishments, visibility, and prominence in a field are all taken into account during the selection process.
Dr. Greasham's distinguished career in the pharmaceutical industry spans more than five decades, marked by a series of influential roles and significant contributions to scientific advancement. Most recently, he has been engaged as a consultant since his retirement from Merck & Co., a role he has maintained for over 20 years.
Notably, Dr. Greasham's consulting work has extended across national and international boundaries, having worked on projects in places like New Zealand, India, Europe, Great Britain and China. A notable chapter of his consulting career involved collaboration with Scynexis, where he was instrumental in directing the development and scale-up of an anti-fungal project that originated at Merck & Co. Dr. Greasham's leadership facilitated the transition of the developed fermentation process to successful large-scale production, overcoming challenges such as language barriers and international logistics. Dr. Greasham ensured compliance with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration requirements. The resulting product was sold in the U.S. before being acquired by a major European pharmaceutical company. Dr. Greasham oversaw the transfer of the process technology.
Before his consulting endeavors, Dr. Greasham served as the director of fermentation process research at Merck & Co. from 1982 to 2004. During this extensive tenure, he led numerous initiatives that advanced fermentation technology and process optimization within the organization. Dr. Greasham's most notable achievement stems from his significant contributions during this period at Merck & Co., where his expertise and leadership were widely recognized within the field.
Dr. Greasham's academic foundation began with a Bachelor of Arts in biology from the University of Evansville in 1964, followed by a Master of Science in biology from Villanova University in 1967. He then earned a Doctor of Philosophy in microbiology from Hahnemann Medical College of Philadelphia in 1970. His educational pursuits were shaped by an early interest in liberal arts before discovering a passion for science, particularly microbiology, which set him on a path toward scientific research and innovation. After completing his doctorate, Dr. Greasham accepted a postdoctoral position at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to gain experience in industry rather than academia, which broadened his perspective on scientific challenges beyond traditional academic settings.
Throughout his professional journey, Dr. Greasham has been an active member of leading industry organizations, such as the American Chemical Society, the Society for Industrial Microbiology and Biotechnology, and the American Society for Microbiology. These affiliations have provided him with valuable opportunities for collaboration and professional growth while reinforcing his commitment to advancing scientific knowledge.
Beyond his professional achievements, Dr. Greasham has contributed to civic life through various roles, including serving as the president of trustees at his local church and supporting community activities. He has also acted as a science fair judge at both elementary school and college levels, encouraging young minds to pursue scientific inquiry.
Over the course of his career at Merck & Co., Dr. Greasham has received several awards and honors that reflect his impact on industrial microbiology and biotechnology. Mentorship played a pivotal role throughout his education and career, as he attributes much of his success to guidance from exceptional mentors as well as to what he describes as blessings from above. Dr. Greasham's willingness to challenge prevailing academic perceptions about industry work further demonstrates his dedication to fostering understanding between academic and industrial communities.
Looking ahead, Dr. Greasham aims to deepen connections with his entire family by traveling together and engaging more closely with relatives across generations. His enduring legacy is reflected not only in his scientific accomplishments but also in his commitment to mentorship, community service, and family bonds developed over more than half a century in science and industry.
About Marquis Who's Who®:
Since 1899, when A. N. Marquis printed the First Edition of Who's Who in America®, Marquis Who's Who® has chronicled the lives of the most accomplished individuals and innovators from every significant field of endeavor, including politics, business, medicine, law, education, art, religion and entertainment. The suite of Marquis® publications, including Who's Who in America® and Who's Who in the World®, remains an essential biographical source for thousands of researchers, journalists, librarians and executive search firms around the globe. Marquis® publications can be viewed at the official Marquis Who's Who® website,

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Clicklinks | Sanyou Bio Launches Clicklinks, an AI-Driven Innovation Hub for Original Drug Discovery - The Manila Times
Pharma Industry.content:
SHANGHAI
,
Aug. 28, 2026
/PRNewswire/ -- Sanyou Biopharmaceuticals Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Sanyou Bio"), today announced the official launch of Clicklinks, an AI-STAL and SAI-DA powered collaborative network designed to support original drug discovery and preclinical development.
Positioned as an Innovation Hub for Original Drug Discovery, Clicklinks brings together industry partners across the biopharmaceutical value chain to enable more efficient, integrated, and scalable R&D. By combining highly integrated technology platforms with diversified, ecosystem-based collaboration models, the platform aims to accelerate the global development and commercialization of innovative drugs, in line with Sanyou Bio's mission: "To make it easy to develop new drugs worldwide."
Clicklinks: An Open and Collaborative Network Ecosystem
Clicklinks is designed as an open, interconnected, and collaborative network ecosystem that facilitates cooperation among companies, research institutions, and individual innovators with complementary capabilities.
The platform's primary objective is to accelerate the translation and application of high-value projects, technologies, and products by providing a trusted environment for collaboration. Through this approach, Clicklinks will empower its partners in developing "next-generation therapeutics" with the potential to significantly improve patients' quality of life and deliver transformative, potentially curative treatment solutions.

.
Clicklinks: An Integrated Platform Covering the Drug R&D Value Chain
Accessible through a single web-based portal, Clicklinks integrates key stages of drug research and development across six core modules:
Advertisement
Core Reagents - High-quality research tools and materials.
Drug Discovery - Early-stage workflows from target validation to lead optimization.
Pharmacology & Efficacy - Comprehensive in vitro and in vivo preclinical pharmacology evaluation.
Innovative Technologies - Advanced technology platforms supporting new R&D paradigms.
Preclinical Research - Integrated PCC-IND preclinical evaluation.
Disease Frontiers - Insights into emerging disease mechanisms and therapeutic trends.
Through internal innovation and integration across upstream and downstream partners, the platform currently incorporates nearly 70 standardized and modularized technology platforms, with ongoing expansion to meet evolving R&D needs. Clicklinks is designed to provide flexible, efficient, one-stop solutions tailored to diverse development programs.
R&D activities on the platform are guided by clinical demand, with a strategic focus on nine major disease areas: oncology, metabolic diseases, autoimmune diseases, neurology, cardiovascular diseases, infectious diseases, ophthalmology, aging-related diseases, and pet healthcare.
Building on innovative molecular foundations, Clicklinks supports a wide range of therapeutic modalities, including monoclonal antibodies, bispecific antibodies, peptides, nucleic acids, ADCs (antibody-drug conjugates), APCs, AOCs, PDCs, POCs, and cell therapies such as CAR-T.
Flexible and Global Collaboration Models
Advertisement
To enable end-to-end collaboration and global engagement, Clicklinks supports a variety of business and partnership models, including co-development of R&D platforms, establishment of NewCos, joint investments, collaborative development programs, and product and service alliances.
By fostering strategic partnerships across the industry value chain, the platform aims to promote resource sharing, complementary expertise, and collective problem-solving in response to the growing complexity of innovative drug development.
CEO Commentary
Dr. Lang Guojun, CEO of Sanyou Bio, said:"The journey of innovative drug development is long and filled with challenges. Sanyou Bio is committed to building an industry-leading, integrated drug R&D platform and, through excellence in scientific innovation and business operations, aspiring to become a global leader in innovative drug development. By working closely with partners across the industry, Sanyou Bio is dedicated to fulfilling its mission: "To make it easy to develop new drugs worldwide".
Advertisement
We firmly believe that Clicklinks, our Innovation Hub for Original Drug Discovery, will enable us to support our partners more consistently and effectively in achieving major breakthroughs across their drug development programs. We also look forward to collaborating with more like-minded partners to foster an open, connected, and mutually beneficial innovation ecosystem-accelerating the delivery of breakthrough therapies to patients around the world."
About Sanyou
Sanyou Biopharmaceuticals is a high-tech biopharmaceutical company driven by the mission of "To make it easy to develop new drugs worldwide". The company is committed to fundamentally addressing the key challenges at the source of innovative drug development.
Powered by its AI-STAL and supported by Sanyou AI-Drug Accelerator（SAI-DA）, Sanyou provides one-stop comprehensive solutions to tackle all challenges in molecular generation and innovative drug R&D.
Advertisement
Sanyou Bio has been dedicated to developing a world-class innovative biological drug R&D hub and to working collaboratively with partners worldwide to accelerate the development of innovative therapeutics.
Headquartered in Shanghai, China, Sanyou has established global business centers across Asia, North America, and Europe, forming an international business network. The company currently operates and has planned over 20,000 square meters of R&D and GMP facilities.
Sanyou has established strong collaborations with more than 2,000 pharmaceutical and biotech companies worldwide, empowering over 1,200 new drug discovery and development projects. It has completed more than 50 collaboration projects, over 10 of which have advanced to IND approval and clinical development stages.
The company has filed over 170 invention patents, with more than 30 granted. It has also obtained over 10 national and international qualifications and system certifications, including National High-Tech Enterprise, Shanghai "Specialized and Innovative" Enterprise, ISO9001, and ISO27001.

Pharma Policy.content:
By
Suzanne Blake
Reporter
0

A federal appeals court has dealt another blow to the pharmaceutical industry's effort to stop
Medicare's drug price negotiation program,
ruling in favor of the federal government and upholding key provisions of the
Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).
The decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit on Wednesday rejected a lawsuit brought by the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and other groups challenging the constitutionality of Medicare drug price negotiations.
The ruling is the latest in a series of courtroom defeats for drugmakers seeking to halt the program, which allows Medicare to negotiate the prices of certain high-cost prescription medications used by seniors.
Read More
on
Business
Why It Matters
Prescription drug costs
remain one of the biggest financial concerns for older Americans. The Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program was created under the Inflation Reduction Act signed into law in 2022 and is intended to reduce costs for beneficiaries and taxpayers by allowing the government to negotiate prices directly with drug manufacturers.
The pharmaceutical industry has argued that the program unfairly pressures companies into accepting government-set prices and could discourage future innovation. But many lawmakers and beneficiaries believe the policy is necessary to address decades of rising prescription drug costs.
...
What to Know
On Wednesday, the Fifth Circuit affirmed a lower-court decision that rejected arguments from PhRMA, the National Infusion Center Association and the Global Colon Cancer Association.
The plaintiffs argued that the Medicare negotiation program violated constitutional protections, including due process guarantees and limits on government power.
However, Judge Leslie Southwick, writing for the court, said that drug manufacturers do not have a protected right to sell medicines to Medicare beneficiaries at prices of their choosing because participation in Medicare and Medicaid is voluntary.
“We agree with the Second Circuit, which rejected another IRA due process challenge on the grounds that a ‘company suffers no deprivation of its property interests by voluntarily submitting to a price-regulated government program,’” Southwick wrote.
The ruling follows similar setbacks for other industry company challengers like Merck and AstraZeneca, as well as lawsuits supported by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
The U.S. Supreme Court declined earlier this year to take up several challenges to the program.
“This ruling is significant in removing another potential legal obstacle to Medicare negotiating lower prices for some of the program’s most expensive prescription drugs, making it increasingly likely that negotiated pricing will remain part of Medicare in the future,” Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor at the University of Tennessee at Martin, told
Newsweek
.
Related Story
Medicare Update: List of Insurers Denying the Most Patients Standard Care
What Was the Ruling on Medicare Drug Price Negotiations?
The Fifth Circuit found that drugmakers lack a protected property interest in selling medications to Medicare beneficiaries at preferred prices because participation in the program is voluntary.
The court also rejected arguments that:
Congress improperly delegated authority to federal health officials.
The IRA's excise tax on companies that decline to negotiate amounts to an unconstitutional excessive fine.
The program violates manufacturers' due process rights.
In its opinion, the court wrote that the financial importance of Medicare sales does not amount to legal compulsion, even if companies have strong economic incentives to participate.
“Ultimately, this is about the balance between affordability and innovation,” Beene said. “Lower negotiated prices can reduce what seniors and taxpayers spend and potentially improve medication usage, while pharmaceutical companies argue that restricting the revenue generated by successful drugs could eventually reduce investment in developing new treatments.”
How Does This Affect Seniors?
For Medicare beneficiaries, the ruling means that the drug price negotiation program will continue operating while legal challenges proceed.
The program is designed to lower the cost of certain high-spending prescription drugs covered by Medicare, potentially reducing out-of-pocket expenses for many seniors.
“The Inflation Reduction Act brought Medicare drug-price negotiations to the forefront,” Kevin Thompson, the CEO of 9i Capital Group and the host of the
9innings
podcast, told
Newsweek
. “For the first time, Medicare was given the authority to directly negotiate prices on certain high-cost prescription drugs.”
The program could make prescription medicines more affordable and lessen the financial burden on older Americans, many of whom rely on expensive treatments for chronic conditions.
“The real health question is whether someone takes the drug their doctor prescribed. Or quietly stretches it, delays a refill, or skips it because of the price,” Michael Ryan, a finance expert and the founder of MichaelRyanMoney.com, told
Newsweek
. “Lower prices can't guarantee better health, but they can remove one very real barrier to taking medication as prescribed.”
Under the ruling, no benefits or drug coverage will change, but the government's ability to continue negotiating prices has been reinforced under the law.
What Drugs Were Named in the Lawsuit?
The PhRMA lawsuit primarily challenged the structure and legality of the Medicare negotiation program itself rather than focusing on a single medicine. The case was brought by PhRMA along with the National Infusion Center Association and the Global Colon Cancer Association.
“Pharmaceutical companies are claiming that participation in these programs is essentially involuntary and argue that pricing drugs this way is not a fair business practice,” Thompson said. “The ruling against the pharmaceutical industry is a blow, given that the court disagreed with the argument that participation is involuntary and instead suggested that it is voluntary for these companies to participate in the programs.”
What Is PhRMA and Why Did It Sue?
PhRMA is the leading trade organization representing many of the nation's largest pharmaceutical companies.
The group sued in 2023, arguing that the IRA's drug pricing provisions violated constitutional protections. Among other claims, the organization contended that the law lacked sufficient checks and balances and imposed an overly punitive excise tax on manufacturers that declined to participate in negotiations.
The industry has long argued that the negotiations effectively coerce participation because of Medicare's importance to the pharmaceutical market. But courts so far have repeatedly rejected that argument.
Not everyone agrees, though.
“The reality is that the pharmaceutical industry needs access to the prescription drug market through Medicare and Medicaid,” Thompson said. “If companies were to simply remove their drugs from these programs, cheaper alternatives could potentially take their place and drive prices down even further. That could be great for the consumer, but bad for the pharmaceutical industry.”
Newsweek
reached out to PhRMA for comment.
What Happens Next
PhRMA said it is reviewing the Fifth Circuit's decision and evaluating its options.
While the organization may seek a possible appeal to the Supreme Court, the latest decision adds to a growing series of judicial victories for the government.
“This ruling is mostly positive for beneficiaries because keeping expensive medications affordable can have real health consequences when people are less likely to skip prescriptions,” Beene said.

Experts call for balanced drug policy to keep medicines affordable

The World Health Organization’s (WHO) essential medicines list contains 532 medicines for adults, while Bangladesh’s national essential medicines list has only 117.
TBS Report
25 August, 2026, 03:45 pm
Last modified: 26 August, 2026, 12:15 am
Patents for pharmaceutical and agrochemical products are limited according to TRIPS Council rules. Photo: TBS
Public health experts have called for a balanced drug policy that keeps essential medicines affordable and accessible while ensuring manufacturers can sustainably produce and supply quality drugs.
The government should adopt a science-based essential medicines list, ensure sustainable pricing, review prices regularly, prevent supply disruptions, and strengthen financial protection for patients, they said at the National Policy Dialogue 2026.
The event, titled "Medicines Within Patients' Reach, Sustainability of Manufacturers: Towards a Balanced Drug Policy," was organised by the Public Integrity Network for Evidence and Transparency in Dhaka today (25 August).
Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel
Affordability and industry sustainability are not conflicting goals but two essential objectives of the same public health policy, said Professor Syed Abdul Hamid of the University of Dhaka and convener of the Alliance for Health Reforms Bangladesh.
"A drug policy shouldn't aim for the lowest possible price; it should establish a sustainable price that patients can afford while enabling manufacturers to produce quality medicines," he said.
According to the keynote paper, Bangladesh has regulated
117 essential medicines
under a cost-plus pricing formula since 1994. However, prices have not been regularly reviewed and have remained unchanged since 2022, widening the gap between production costs and prices amid rising costs of raw materials, fuel, labour, packaging and transport.
An initiative to expand the
essential medicines list to 295
and introduce a new pricing structure was taken in
February 2026
but scrapped in August before implementation.
Prof Hamid said the move should not create policy uncertainty, urging policymakers to learn from past experience and develop a more realistic, evidence-based drug policy.
He said access to medicines depends not only on price but also on availability, affordability, physical accessibility, and quality and appropriate use. Irrational drug use,
over-the-counter sales
, and weak financial protection for patients must also be addressed.
Public health expert Dr M Mushtuq Husain called for price controls aligned with universal health coverage while protecting the domestic pharmaceutical industry from unfair competition.
WHO Representative and Mission Head Dr Mamunur Rahman Malik said the WHO updates its Essential Medicines List every two years, while Bangladesh has revised its list only five or six times since 1984.
"Science is not static," he said, calling for regular pharmaceutical sector assessments and stronger drug regulatory capacity.
Dr Abu Mohammad Zakir Hossain, a member of the Health Reform Commission, said medicine prices should not be increased through packaging improvements.
Meanwhile, Mohammad Mizanur Rahman, treasurer of the Bangladesh Association of Pharmaceutical Industries, warned that excessive price controls could discourage local production.
Syed S Kaiser Kabir, CEO of Renata, suggested that the government provide direct subsidies or free medicines to poor patients instead of putting artificial pressure on manufacturers to cut prices.
He also said Bangladesh's medicine prices are lower than in many other countries, noting that Renata exports to more than 60 countries, most of which do not impose direct price controls. He called for reassessing how uninterrupted supply can be ensured while maintaining strict price controls.

Headlines
DRAP ordered to overhaul of drug pricing rules, curb unjustified medicine price hikes
Minister for Economic Affairs directs review of importer margins running as high as 40%, adds health economist to DRAP board
News Desk
August 28, 2026
3
min read
Size
A
A
A

A

A
Font
Sans Serif
Serif
Classic
Modern
Full screen
Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Establishment Division Ahad Cheema has directed the Ministry of National Health Services and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) to urgently revise the regulatory framework governing drug pricing, including changes to the Hardship Policy and the composition of the DRAP Policy Board, with a focus on protecting consumers from unjustified price increases while keeping essential medicines available.
Chairing a meeting on drug pricing, Cheema expressed dissatisfaction with DRAP's existing formula for calculating medicine price increases, calling for a comprehensive review to ensure any revision is transparent, evidence-based and fully justified.
He directed DRAP to strengthen the formula with greater scrutiny and independent checks so that cost pressures are not automatically passed on to consumers.
Cheema instructed the Secretary of National Health Services and DRAP's CEO to finalise revised Hardship Policy rules at the earliest opportunity for presentation to the relevant approval forum.
He stressed that the framework must ensure hardship provisions offer relief only in genuine cases, rather than becoming a route for shifting disproportionate commercial costs onto patients.
The minister also directed a revision of the DRAP Policy Board's composition to strengthen expertise and evidence-based decision-making, specifically calling for the inclusion of a health economist and a public health expert.
Both the health ministry and DRAP agreed to the proposal, and Cheema instructed officials to begin the process and submit the changes for approval promptly.
"Drug-pricing decisions have a direct impact on millions of households. Our regulatory framework must therefore combine pharmaceutical sustainability with affordability and strong consumer protection," Cheema said.
DRAP officials briefed the minister on the existing Hardship Policy and its application to essential medicines. Cheema noted that importers often seek relief under the policy while simultaneously requesting price increases, and said the revised rules must ensure that benefits granted under the Hardship Policy are reflected in pricing rather than adding further burden on consumers.
He said importers already benefiting from tax concessions or other government relief under the Hardship Policy should be prepared to rationalise their own margins instead of passing the full cost onto consumers. Cheema directed DRAP to examine existing importer and retailer margins — which can run as high as 40% in some cases — and provide for their rationalisation under the revised rules.
"If the Government is extending relief under the Hardship Policy, the importer and retailer must also share the burden through reasonable adjustment of their margins. This adjustment should take place within the supply chain and must not, under any circumstances, be passed on to the consumer," Cheema said, directing officials to build a mechanism for margin rationalisation into the proposed rules and submit the revised framework promptly for approval.
The minister said the regulator bears responsibility for maintaining fair market balance — keeping essential medicines available while protecting patients from unjustified price hikes — adding that commercial viability, while important, cannot come at the expense of consumers.
The meeting also reviewed pricing mechanisms for originator and existing brands. DRAP officials said reference pricing, based on prices in neighbouring and other relevant countries, is currently used for originator brands.
Cheema said this international reference pricing should be backed by an independent verification mechanism to ensure decisions rest on credible data reflecting actual market conditions.
He directed DRAP to build a stronger, more independent system of checks within the pricing framework to ensure transparency and effective oversight, adding that a sustainable pharmaceutical market must go hand in hand with affordability and protection of public interest.
Cheema said the government, under Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif, remains committed to providing maximum relief to the public, stressing that access to affordable medicines is directly tied to public welfare and that regulatory mechanisms would continue to be strengthened to balance the pharmaceutical sector's needs with consumer interests.
Secretary National Health Services Muhammad Mehmood (Retd Captain), DRAP CEO Dr Obaidullah, DRAP's Director Pricing, and other senior officials attended the meeting.

Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Establishment Division Senator Ahad Cheema directed the Ministry of National Health Services and DRAP to urgently review the existing pricing formula, including the Hardship Policy and the composition of the DRAP Policy Board.
Cheema said the current mechanism for determining medicine price increases requires a comprehensive review. He directed DRAP to introduce greater scrutiny and independent checks so that cost pressures are not automatically passed on to consumers through higher medicine prices.

Cheema further directed that a Health Economist and a Public Health expert be included on the DRAP Policy Board to strengthen expertise and evidence based decision making. DRAP and the Ministry of National Health Services agreed with the proposed changes.
The meeting also examined importer and retailer margins. Cheema said importers that receive tax concessions or other government relief under the Hardship Policy should also consider rationalizing their own margins rather than passing the full cost on to consumers. DRAP was directed to examine existing margins, including cases where they may be around 40 percent, and propose adjustments under the revised rules.
The meeting also reviewed pricing mechanisms for originator and existing brands. DRAP officials said originator brands currently use international reference pricing based on prices in neighboring and other relevant countries. Cheema directed DRAP to introduce independent verification of international reference prices and strengthen checks within the overall drug pricing system.
Cheema said drug pricing decisions directly affect millions of households and that the regulatory framework must balance the sustainability of the pharmaceutical sector with medicine affordability and consumer protection.

Pharma Policy.url_match_title: CMS’ proposed cuts to 340B drug program will hurt rural health - WV News
Pharma Policy.content:
A cancer patient in a rural West Virginia county should not have to drive past a shuttered clinic to reach the nearest one still open. Yet that is the trajectory some in Washington are pushing West Virginia toward, one funding cut at a time.
In early July, the Centers for and Medicaid Services (CMS) published its proposed 2027 Medicare outpatient prospective payment system (OPPS) rule, which includes a proposal to reduce Medicare Part B reimbursement for separately payable 340B drugs by more than 37% for most 340B hospitals. When we talk about funding cuts affecting health care delivery, this proposed cut is brutal because it would affect only those safety-net hospitals with 340B pharmacies. In West Virginia, that could be close to 40 hospitals and all their patients who rely on 340B pharmacies to afford their medications.
I sincerely hope our Congressional delegation is paying attention to these cuts and will step up to protect West Virginians. When debating health care policy, the most important question is not who wins politically. It is whether a policy helps patients receive timely, effective care while using limited resources wisely. By that standard, protecting the 340B drug discount program should be a priority in West Virginia.
As a legislator responsible for health policy and a health care executive, I look for measurable results: shorter travel times, more available appointments, fewer avoidable emergency-room visits and financially stable providers. In communities where one hospital or health system may be the only lifeline, those measures have real consequences. They determine whether a neighbor can receive cancer treatment near home, find behavioral health care or fill a prescription without missing work.
Congress created 340B in 1992 so eligible hospitals and clinics could purchase outpatient medicines at discounted prices and stretch scarce resources to serve more patients. Manufacturers voluntarily choose whether to participate in Medicaid; if they do, they must agree to provide these discounts. 340B requires no new state appropriation or higher local tax bill; it simply makes existing health care dollars work harder.
That matters here. West Virginia faces perpetual shortages in health care providers and access to facilities, and we all know rural providers are at risk of having to close their doors. When a service disappears at a rural hospital, patients cannot simply choose another facility down the street. They may have to drive an hour or longer, postpone care or go without it entirely.
Across the state, 340B savings can help sustain oncology, behavioral health, specialty clinics, pharmacy services and transportation assistance. It allows providers to purchase much-needed equipment, maintain staff, perform more procedures and do all of this at zero cost to the taxpayer. Cuts to 340B would result in the giant pharmaceutical companies padding their profits, all while West Virginians would see shuttered clinics and increased prices.
When it comes to 340B policy, the test is straightforward: Would a proposed change make essential care more available, affordable and sustainable? If the answer is no — or the consequences are unknown — policymakers should proceed cautiously. Rebuilding a closed rural service or replacing a departed clinician is far more expensive than preserving that capacity.
Improving health outcomes requires smart public policy that turns limited resources into better care. That means supporting proven tools and giving local providers flexibility to meet community needs. By helping safety-net providers sustain services close to home without new taxpayer spending, 340B reflects the kind of practical, results-driven policy West Virginia needs.
I hope Sen. Shelley Moore Capito leads our delegation in the fight to prevent CMS’s planned cuts to the 340B program so it remains a fiscally responsible tool that helps safety-net providers stretch resources without additional taxpayer spending. When there is so much that divides us, this is something that can easily bring us all together. It is a practical investment in healthier communities and a stronger rural health care system.

Pharma Policy.content:
HEALTHCARE
U.S. Food and Drug Administration
Add Topic
Eli Lilly's diabetes drug Mounjaro gets approval for a new use
Ken Alltucker
USA TODAY
Aug. 28, 2026, 1:40 p.m. ET
Hear this story
The Food and Drug Administration approved Eli Lilly's
diabetes drug Mounjaro
to cut down the risk of heart attack or stroke in high-risk adults with Type 2 diabetes.
The approval gives consumers another option
when seeking a GLP-1 medication
to lower heart-related health risk. In 2024, the FDA approved Novo Nordisk's anti-obesity drug, Wegovy, to lower the risk of cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke in overweight or obese adults without diabetes.
Mounjaro is Lilly's diabetes drug that targets the GIP and GLP-1 hormone receptors. The drug is also prescribed for weight loss under the brand name Zepbound.
Eli Lilly said Mounjaro's approval to reduce risk of heart attack and stroke followed a large study comparing the drug to Lilly's older diabetes drug Trulicity.
The approval was based on results from a trial that showed Mounjaro outperformed Trulicity in reducing the risk of major heart events. The study showed those who took Mounjaro had an 8% lower rate of cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke, Lilly said.
Lilly, Novo and other drugmakers are studying GLP-1 medications for a variety of conditions as well as a new generation of more powerful weight less medications.
Lilly said a study showed people on its experimental, next-generation
weight-loss shot
retatrutide achieved weight loss of 19% to 28%. The results for some people were
on par with weight-loss surgery
. Retatrutide works differently than existing medications because it mimics three hormones − GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon triple hormone receptor agonists.
In a recent report, Wells Fargo said the
pipeline of GLP-1 weight-loss medications now surpasses
cancer drugs as the most valuable category of products on the horizon. Goldman Sachs projects global sales of weight-loss medications will be about $105 billion by 2030.
Medicare has
started coverage of GLP-1s for older adults
under the bridge program, but some employers and insurers are balking at paying for the weight-loss medications. Starbucks, for example, said it
would no longer cover
the cost of GLP-1 weight-loss medications for employees beginning in October.
A recent survey from the benefits consultant Mercer found about 6% of large employers expect to drop coverage of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs in 2026 and an additional 5% plan to drop coverage in 2027. Nearly half of large employers covered the weight loss drugs in 2025.
However, insurers are more likely to cover GLP-1 drugs when prescribed for Type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea or to reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke.

Pharma Policy.content:
three dosages of mounjaro pens in front of anatomical hearts fading mounjaro approved for decreasing heart disease risks for those with type 2 diabetes.
Eli Lilly; Everyday Health
Key Takeaways
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has authorized Mounjaro (tirzepatide) to prevent cardiovascular emergencies in high-risk adults with type 2 diabetes.
The drug benefits heart health by reducing obesity and excess weight, lowering blood pressure, and improving cholesterol levels.
Up to 1 in 3 adults with type 2 diabetes may have undetected cardiovascular disease.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide)
, the popular injectable GLP-1/GIP drug, is already prescribed to lower blood sugar in people with
type 2 diabetes
. Now the medication has won authorization by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to prevent heart attack and stroke in high-risk patients with type 2 diabetes.
As many as 1 in 3 adults in the United States with type 2 diabetes are estimated to have undetected cardiovascular disease, research suggests.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"Cardiovascular disease is one of the most common causes of death in patients affected by type 2 diabetes," says
Peminda Cabandugama, MD
, an endocrinologist with the Cleveland Clinic and a spokesperson for The Obesity Society who was not involved in Mounjaro's development. "This approval is in keeping with the direct action of GLP-1 medications and their combinations in reducing this risk."
Mounjaro Joins the Lineup of Diabetes Meds Showing Heart Health Benefits
Mounjaro works by mimicking the natural gut hormones GLP-1 and GIP, improving blood sugar levels and reducing appetite.
Studies have shown that GLP-1 medications benefit heart health by promoting weight loss and lowering blood pressure, LDL (bad) cholesterol, and triglycerides (a very common type of fat in the blood).
Another injectable GLP-1 diabetes medication on the market, Ozempic (semaglutide), was approved in 2020 for cardiovascular risk reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes. The GLP-1 medication Trulicity (dulaglutide) was also approved in 2020 to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke in people with type 2 diabetes with or without established cardiovascular disease.
Mounjaro Beat Trulicity in Trial Results
The FDA approval was based on results looking at cardiovascular outcomes with Mounjaro and Trulicity, in a trial involving more than 13,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease who were followed for an average of four years.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Mounjaro demonstrated an 8 percent lower rate of cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke compared with Trulicity.
The results of the trial demonstrate "meaningful risk reduction" for Mounjaro according to
Marilyn Tan, MD
, clinical professor of medicine, endocrinology, gerontology and metabolism at Stanford Medicine in Palo Alto, California, who was not involved in the drug development.
Will the FDA Action Expand Insurance Coverage for Mounjaro?
Whether this new FDA authorization will change insurance coverage remains to be seen.
"This new indication may improve and/or expand insurance coverage for such medications, but GLP-1 agonists remain costly, so it's ultimately up to the individual insurance plans on how they provide coverage," says Dr. Tan.
EDITORIAL SOURCES
Everyday Health follows strict sourcing guidelines to ensure the accuracy of its content, outlined in our
editorial policy
. We use only trustworthy sources, including peer-reviewed studies, board-certified medical experts, patients with lived experience, and information from top institutions.

Medicare’s 2027 Drug Deductible Is $700, Up $85. You Pay All of It Before Your Plan Pays Anything.
Medicare's Part D deductible is climbing again in 2027, and what your plan actually charges you in January depends on details buried inside documents most enrollees never read before auto-renewal locks them in.
By
Gerelyn Terzo
Published August 28, 2026, 8:01pm ET · 3 min read
The Full Benefits Desk
desk. Editor:
Gerelyn Terzo
.
𝕏
f
⧉
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A calendar marks December 7 as the crucial end date for Medicare open enrollment, highlighting the importance of timely decisions regarding supplemental coverage like Medigap.
© CLS Digital Arts / Shutterstock.com
Medicare’s
annual open enrollment begins October 15
, and there is a new amount worth knowing before the renewal notice gets tossed into the paperwork pile. The standard Part D deductible for 2027 is $700, up from $615 this year.
That $85 increase is already settled. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) finalized it in April, along with a higher $2,400 annual out-of-pocket threshold for covered Part D drugs. What is not settled for every retiree is whether the plan they choose will actually make them pay the full $700. That distinction is where the shopping begins.
$700 Is the Standard, Not Everyone’s Bill
Under Medicare’s standard Part D design, the beneficiary pays 100% of covered drug costs subject to the deductible until $700 has been met. After that comes the initial coverage phase, where the standard design generally calls for 25% cost sharing. But insurers have room to offer something better.
Some Part D plans reduce or eliminate the standard deductible. Others may apply it to higher-cost tiers while covering certain lower-tier drugs before the deductible is satisfied. That means two plans can both carry Medicare Part D coverage while giving the same retiree a very different January pharmacy bill.
Certain drugs also have their own federal protections. Covered insulin products and recommended adult vaccines are not simply treated like an ordinary brand-name prescription waiting behind the full standard deductible. So the useful question is not, “How am I going to pay $700?” It is, “How does my 2027 plan apply the deductible to the drugs I actually take?”
The Bigger Ceiling Is Rising Too
The deductible is not the only number moving. In 2027, the annual Part D out-of-pocket threshold rises to $2,400 from $2,100 in 2026. Once a beneficiary reaches that limit through qualifying covered-drug spending, cost sharing falls to $0 for the rest of the calendar year.
The $700 deductible counts toward that journey. It is not $700 on top of another $2,400. That matters for someone using expensive prescriptions throughout the year. The maximum protected exposure for covered Part D drugs is rising by $300, but the ceiling remains firmly in place. A high-cost medication can still make January painful without leaving the retiree exposed to unlimited covered-drug bills through December.
Auto-Renewal Can Hide More Than the Deductible
If a current plan continues into 2027 and the enrollee does nothing during open enrollment, coverage will generally roll over. The name on the card may stay the same while several numbers underneath it change. A prescription can move to another tier. A preferred pharmacy can lose that status. Copays and coinsurance can shift. The deductible itself can be structured differently. That is why comparing premiums alone misses the point.
A plan charging a few dollars more each month could cost less over the full year if it gives favorable treatment to the medications someone actually uses. The reverse can happen just as easily. CMS will release finalized 2027 plan information before open enrollment, which runs from October 15 through December 7. The deductible is only the most visible line item; IRMAA surcharges and coverage gaps can add thousands more, which is why we mapped the full set of Medicare cost traps in a
free guide here
.
Give the $700 Bump Some Time Before December 7
Once 2027 plans are available, consider these steps:
Enter every prescription, dose and preferred pharmacy into Medicare Plan Finder and compare total annual spending, not just monthly premiums.
Check whether each plan applies the full $700 deductible, a smaller one or no deductible to the drug tiers you use.
Look at the formulary and pharmacy network again even if you intend to keep the same plan. Last year’s good fit does not guarantee next year’s.
Someone taking only inexpensive generics may barely notice the $85 increase. A retiree filling an expensive brand-name prescription could feel it much sooner. The $700 figure is worth knowing. The smarter question is whether your plan makes you pay all of it, and what happens to the pharmacy bill after you do.

Pharma Policy.url_match_title: People Took GLP-1 Drugs to Lose Weight. Researchers Are Finding Much More Benefits - Yahoo Health
Pharma Policy.content:
GLP-1
Millions of people know GLP-1 medications as powerful weight-loss drugs, but researchers are uncovering a much bigger and more complicated story about what these medicines may do inside the body.
11% of American adults are currently taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss alone, according to
Gallup
, and that number does not include people using them for diabetes or other medical conditions. Although the drug class has been used clinically for about two decades, medications like Ozempic and Wegovy have recently become symbols of a much broader conversation about health, disease prevention, and the future of medicine.
The biggest question now is no longer just how much weight these drugs can help people lose.
Researchers are investigating whether GLP-1 medications may also affect conditions involving the heart, kidneys, liver, sleep, addiction and even cancer risk.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Some of those findings have already changed medical practice, while others remain early-stage research that requires much more evidence.
Understanding the difference is becoming increasingly important as excitement around these medications continues to grow.
More Than an Appetite Drug
These medications work on far more of the body than most people realize. That's a significant part of why researchers keep finding effects beyond weight loss.
GLP-1 stands for glucagon-like peptide-1, a hormone naturally released by the small intestine after eating. It helps trigger insulin production,
slows food movement through the stomach,
and signals the brain that the body has had enough food. GLP-1 medications mimic that hormone, but their effects may extend beyond appetite control.
That is because GLP-1 receptors are found throughout the body, including in the brain, heart, kidneys, blood vessels, lungs and thyroid. Researchers believe this wide distribution helps explain why the medications are being studied for conditions far beyond obesity and diabetes.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Dr. Robert Kushner, founder of the American Board of Obesity Medicine, described the broader impact of the drug class by pointing to "a range of systemic health benefits of GLP-1 medications that are
linked to their anti-inflammatory properties
, metabolic enhancement and mechanical benefits."
The medications first became important as diabetes treatments roughly 20 years ago. The current scientific focus is on understanding how many other systems they may influence.
What the Science Has Already Established
Some benefits associated with GLP-1 medications are no longer just theories. Several uses have already received FDA approval.
Heart health was one of the earliest areas where the conversation expanded. Wegovy is approved to
reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke
in adults with established heart disease and excess weight. At the same time, Ozempic has a similar approval for people with
Type 2 diabetes and kidney disease
.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Sleep apnea became another major development when Zepbound became the first FDA-approved
medication for obstructive sleep apnea
. Clinical trials showed meaningful reductions in breathing disruptions among people taking the drug.
The list has continued to grow. Ozempic is now approved to
reduce the risk of worsening chronic kidney disease
and cardiovascular death in certain patients. Wegovy is also approved for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, known as MASH, in adults with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis.
Scientists are still debating how much of these improvements come from weight loss itself and how much comes from other biological effects. A study co-authored by Dr. Harlan Krumholz of Yale found tirzepatide lowered systolic blood pressure by nearly seven points compared with placebo. Other research found semaglutide reduced cardiovascular inflammation even among people who had not experienced major weight loss.
"The weight loss is not fully explaining what's going on,"
Krumholz said to Today
. "The benefits of these GLP-1s extend beyond the weight loss."
The Cancer Numbers Are Striking, But Researchers Are Being Careful
Early studies have produced attention-grabbing results, but scientists warn that promising associations are not proof.
Advertisement
Advertisement
A 2026 study linked GLP-1 use with a
41% lower risk of developing obesity-related cancers
among non-diabetic patients taking the medications for weight loss. Another study presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting found that women with excess weight who used GLP-1 medications were about
30 percent less likely to develop breast cancer
than nonusers.
Those findings have generated interest, but researchers are emphasizing caution.
Researchers behind the 2026 cancer study also noted that reducing cancer risk should not currently be a standalone reason to prescribe GLP-1 medications.
Dr. Elizabeth McDonald, who led the breast cancer research, described the findings as a
reason for further investigation
rather than a final answer. The drugs affect "many different targets and pathways associated with cancer development," she said. "So we're eager to study them in this context."
Advertisement
Advertisement
Related:
7 Common Weight Loss Myths You Should Stop Believing
The Addiction Finding Nobody Expected
Image Credit: marevgenna via shutterstock
People taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and weight loss began reporting unexpected changes, including
reduced alcohol cravings
, fewer cigarette urges and less desire for certain compulsive behaviors.
Researchers began studying the pattern
more formally. Clinical trials found GLP-1 medications may reduce alcohol cravings and consumption in controlled settings. In contrast, research involving veterans with Type 2 diabetes found GLP-1 use was consistently associated with lower risks across several substance-use disorders.
GLP-1 medications are not FDA-approved treatments for substance-use disorders. Any future role would likely be considered alongside established approaches such as therapy, peer support, and comprehensive addiction care.
Side Effects, Costs and the Questions That Remain
The excitement around GLP-1 medications is real, but so are the unanswered questions about long-term use.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The most commonly reported side effects involve the digestive system, including nausea, stomach pain, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting. More serious potential concerns include thyroid tumors, pancreatitis, and gallbladder problems. Some patients have also reported muscle loss, possible vision changes, and emotional effects sometimes described as an
"Ozempic personality,"
involving reduced pleasure or emotional engagement.
Access remains another challenge. Cost and insurance coverage continue to limit availability, especially when GLP-1 medications are being considered for conditions beyond their current approvals.
Kushner identified one of medicine's biggest remaining questions: "which patients benefit most, at what dose and for how long."
GLP-1 medications have moved from being viewed primarily as diabetes and weight-loss drugs to becoming one of the most closely studied drug classes in modern medicine. Whether they eventually transform care across multiple diseases will depend on what researchers discover next.

Pharma Policy.content:
Talking with Thalia
New FDA-Approved Drug Offers New Hope for Advanced Pancreatic Cancer Patients
A new once-daily oral medication,
Razon Q
, has received FDA approval for certain patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer who have not responded to previous treatments or cannot undergo traditional therapies. Developed by Revolution Medicines, the drug targets
RAS mutations
, which play a major role in many pancreatic cancer cases. In a large clinical trial, patients receiving the treatment lived about twice as long as those receiving standard chemotherapy. Doctors are calling the results a potential turning point and a game changer in pancreatic cancer treatment. The manufacturer says a 30-day supply will cost wholesalers nearly
$40,000
, although patients' out-of-pocket costs will vary based on insurance coverage, Medicare or Medicaid eligibility, and available financial assistance programs.

Fact check: Abdul El-Sayed attacks Mike Rogers over pharma industry ties

by Matt Mencarini, Bridge Michigan
August 28, 2026

  • Mike Rogers’ campaign sent Abdul El-Sayed a cease and desist letter in June, demanding that he stop calling Rogers a ‘pharma lobbyist’
  • El-Sayed has continued to criticize Rogers for his connections to, and campaign donations from, the pharmaceutical industry
  • During his time in the US House, from 2001-2015, Rogers had been an advocate of increased access to pain meds

Democratic US Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed continues to attack Republican rival Mike Rogers over his connections to the pharmaceutical industry, including hundreds of thousands in past campaign contributions and sponsorship of legislation to expand access to prescription pain medication. 

The sparring began months ago when El-Sayed called Rogers a lobbyist for the drug industry and falsely claimed he’d taken “a $14 million payout” for that work, which prompted the Rogers campaign to send a June 22 cease and desist letter demanding that El-Sayed stop and threatening legal action. 

The letter called the description “demonstrably false,” and both state and federal records show Rogers has never registered as a lobbyist of any kind. 

El-Sayed has since tweaked his attack — but not by much.

“This is a guy who's never seen a check from a pharmaceutical lobbyist he didn't want to cash,” El-Sayed told supporters in primary election night speech, noting he was in medical school when Rogers served in Congress. 

Related: 

  • Mike Rogers 2.0: After defeat, GOP Senate hopeful makes new pitch
  • Rogers vs. El-Sayed: 7 issues defining Michigan’s US Senate race
  • Fact check: What happened to Detroit dogs under El-Sayed?

“He sent our campaign a cease and desist for calling him a pharma lobbyist. But I don't know, if it looks like a duck, walks like a duck, smells like a duck. How am I supposed to know it's a goose?”

Rogers’ connections to the pharmaceutical industry are among the claims Bridge Michigan is reviewing in the state’s fiercely competitive US Senate race between El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Rogers, a Republican. The winner will replace longtime Democratic Senator Gary Peters, who is retiring.

So what’s true about Rogers and US drug companies?

The claims

While he’s stopped publicly referring to Rogers as a “pharma lobbyist,” El-Sayed has frequently drawn similar comparisons. 

“So look, forgive me, Mike. I just know that you spend so much time with pharma lobbyists I just thought you were one,” he said in his primary victory speech. “You've taken so much money for them to raise our prescription drug prices, I just thought that you just got in the business.”

He made similar claims last week in a Detroit press conference. 

Rogers has not been a registered lobbyist, but reporting earlier this year from PolitiFact found that before his 2024 Senate run, Rogers received a $30,000 payment from the lobbying firm CGCN Group, which represented more than 50 clients, including drug and medical tech companies.

Rogers campaign spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet told PolitiFact that Rogers did not work on the lobbying side of the firm and instead advised on strategic communications telecommunications issues.

Rogers and pharmaceutical companies

A 2024 Bridge investigation, during Rogers previous run for Senate, found that he was one of the biggest advocates of increased access to pain medications while he was in Congress from 2001-2015.

During that time, only one bill increasing access that he sponsored, co-sponsored or voted for was signed into law. It was the Veterans Pain Care Act of 2008, which was introduced by Minnesota Democrat Tim Walz and had broad bipartisan support. The law mandated that the Department of Veterans Affairs create a comprehensive pain care policy.

In 2003, Rogers introduced the National Pain Care Policy Act in 2003, which began a decade of advocacy by the Republican lawmaker to boost opioid prescriptions, with a goal to “extend accessibility (of pain medications) to more and more Americans suffering from chronic pain.”

Rogers told Bridge he was motivated by personal experience, and recounted how his brother suffered from chronic pain from more than 30 back surgeries, and pain medications were needed to make his life bearable until he died at age 60.

“What we were doing (in Congress) is making sure that true chronic pain sufferers had access to drugs that would at least give some relief and hopefully allow them to spend some time with their family,” he said in 2024. 

Pharma donations

A 2016 investigation by the Associated Press and the Center for Public Integrity found that Rogers’ campaign and leadership accounts received at least $310,000 in contributions from groups tied to the pharmaceutical industry from 2006 to 2015.

At the time, Rogers explained those donations by saying that, “I think they said, ‘This guy is a champion, he’s doing something we believe in and we want to support a guy like that.’”

Donations to Rogers came from companies that agreed to settle litigation from Michigan and other states over their roles in the opioid crisis, Bridge reported in 2024.

During his 2024 run for Senate, Rogers received about $73,276 from donors connected to the pharmaceutical manufacturing, pharmaceutical wholesale, pharmacists or biotech product and research sectors, according to OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks money in politics

All told, Rogers received about $420,000 from donors in the health care sector, with about $105,000 coming from physicians. This cycle, he’s received about $273,000 from the health sector, including $50,000 from “other physician specialists.” 

The bottom line

Rogers was never a registered lobbyist for the pharmaceutical industry, and El-Sayed has stopped publicly calling him one. 

But Rogers has accepted contributions from groups and individuals tied to the pharmaceutical industry in past campaigns and previously advocated for access to opioids for pain management.

Pharma Associations.url_match_title: Marchesini Group showcases pharma and aseptic solutions at CPHI 2026 - Manufacturing Chemist
Pharma Associations.content:
Marchesini Group, a leading manufacturer of complete packaging and filling lines for the pharmaceutical and cosmetics industries, will participate in the next edition of CPHI Worldwide, taking place in Milan from 6 to 8 October 2026. This year’s spotlight will be on the Group’s Pharma and Aseptic Business Units, two strategic divisions that represent Marchesini Group’s excellence in pharmaceutical packaging and advanced technologies for injectable drug manufacturing.
At Stand 9A2, Hall H09, visitors will discover the latest innovations, including a monoblock system for syringe inspection and a compact machine for the automated filling and closing of vials, syringes and cartridges. These solutions will be complemented by systems designed for small-scale production and laboratory applications, developed by Dott. Bonapace, a Group brand that will celebrate its important 80th anniversary during the exhibition. A dedicated area will also be devoted to digital transformation, where visitors will have the opportunity to explore the potential of Morpheus, the predictive maintenance system designed to optimise production performance and enable customers to manage installed machines in an increasingly informed and efficient way.
Among the key events ahead of the exhibition, visitors should not miss the joint presentation by Marchesini Group and SEA Vision, the Group company specialising in vision systems. On 7 October, from 2:45 p.m. to 3:10 p.m., at the Packaging & Device Innovation Theatre, the two teams will showcase their latest innovations in Automated Line Clearance, a key technology for improving automation and efficiency in pharmaceutical production lines.
Technologies on Display
The exhibition area will feature a selection of machines developed by the Group’s various companies to meet the evolving needs of the pharmaceutical industry. Highlights include:
The NSY 200, developed by CMP Phar.ma, is a monoblock machine for the automatic inspection of syringes, equipped with an integrated denesting and renesting unit. Thanks to robotic handling, syringes are transferred to the inspection module in a single row, preventing any contact between them or with metal components. The inspection section can accommodate up to 10 inspection stations, making it possible to control every syringe area, including the flange, stopper, particle detection, fill level, needle shield, glass wall defects, and container integrity through HVLD (High Voltage Leak Detection) technology. The machine also features four customisable rejection lanes for the management of non-conforming syringes.
Manufactured by U.S.-based partner AST, GENiSYS® C is a fully featured fill and close platform with a small, cart-based operational footprint. With the same technology found on AST’s advanced, larger lines, GENiSYS® C has all the power of our innovative solutions for the full scope of drug development, from discovery to commercial distribution.
Among Dott. Bonapace’s key innovations on display will be an OEB5-contained capsule filling machine integrated with an isolator, capable of filling capsules with any solid or liquid oral formulation. The machine combines a compact footprint with advanced technologies and will be showcased alongside its standard monoblock version. Also featured on the stand will be a double-layer rotary tablet press, a compact single-layer tablet press, and a suppository and pessary production line incorporating integrated filling, cooling, sealing, cutting and coding systems. Finally, visitors will be able to see a bench-top blister machine with three independent stations that can thermoform, seal, code and cut in a single seamless cycle.
